MATH9102-CAPhase2-Task2+3-Example

Author

Deirdre Lawless

1. Introduction

This analysis investigates whether key psychological factors, in particular life satisfaction and positive affect, predict the likelihood of an individual being in a relationship controlling for socially desirable responding. A secondary research objective is to evaluate whether this predictive relationship varies across categories of educational attainment. These aims are explored using binary logistic regression.

Two models were fitted:

  • Baseline Model: Life satisfaction and positive affect predicting relationship status controlling for social desirability.

  • Comparison Model: Adds education level to examine whether predictors operate differently across educational groups.

2. Methods

Data were obtained from a psychological well-being survey containing validated scales measuring life satisfaction (Diener et al., 1985), positive affect (Watson et al., 1988), and social desirability (Crowne & Marlowe, 1960). Demographic data—including marital status and education level—were also collected. Relationship status was recoded into a binary variable (0 = not in a relationship; 1 = in a relationship).

Continuous variables were screened for normality using heuristic criteria from Curran, West, and Finch (1996) and Field (2025), whereby standardized skewness and kurtosis values within ±2 and 99.7% of absolute scores within +/- 3.29 indicate approximate normality. Although logistic regression does not assume normality of predictors, these checks guided the selection of appropriate exploratory tests.

Missing data were inspected following Tabachnick and Fidell (2016), and as the proportion and pattern of missingness did not raise concern, listwise deletion was applied.

The analytic workflow was as follows:

  • Data preparation: recoding, screening for missingness, and descriptive analysis.

  • Exploration: t-tests comparing psychological factors across relationship groups and chi-square tests assessing associations with education level.

  • Model fitting: logistic regression using the logit link function.

  • Model evaluation: likelihood-ratio tests, pseudo-R² estimates, and classification performance.

  • Diagnostics: Hosmer–Lemeshow test, variance inflation factors (VIF), and influence statistics (Cook’s distance, leverage, standardized residuals).

  • Interpretation: odds ratios, predicted probabilities, AUC, and confusion matrices.

A significance threshold of p < .05 was applied throughout, and model performance was evaluated using likelihood-ratio tests, pseudo-R² measures, area under the ROC curve (AUC), and classification accuracy. All analyses adhered to best-practice guidance for regression modelling, including assumption checking and inspection of influential observations.

3. Data Preparation and Exploration Results

All psychological variables can be considered to follow an approximately normal distribution (Appendix 1). Standardized skewness and kurtosis values generally fell within recommended limits (Curran et al., 1996) and 99.7% of absolute scores within +/- 3.29. Measures of central tendency and variability indicated adequate spread across all continuous variables.

Marital status was recoded from the original eight categories into a binary categorical variable 0 not in a relationship, 1 in a relationship.

Education levels were unevenly distributed, with some very small categories. “Primary education” was removed due to insufficient sample size.

Independent-samples t-tests examined differences between respondents in a relationship and those not in a relationship (see Appendix 1):

  • Life satisfaction was significantly higher among respondents in a relationship, t(427) = −4.22, p < .001, η² = .04.

  • Positive affect did not differ significantly between groups, t(427) = −1.07, p = .28.

  • Social desirability was slightly but significantly higher among those in relationships, t(427) = −2.77, p = .006, η² = .02.

A chi-square test demonstrated a small association between relationship status and educational attainment, χ²(4, N = 429) = 20.17, p < .001, φ = .22.

Together, these results justify inclusion of psychological and educational variables in the regression models.

4. Baseline Model : Pyschological Predictors Only

4.1 Model Fit

A binary logistic regression model was built to examine whether life satisfaction and positive affect could be considered to predict relationship status controlling for socially desirable responding. The overall model was statistically significant, χ²(3, N = 429) = 23.92, p < .001, indicating the predictors reliably distinguished between respondents in and out of relationships. Pseudo-R² values indicated modest explanatory power:

  • Cox–Snell R² = .054

  • Nagelkerke R² = .075

-Tjur’s R² = .055

Together, these values indicate that the predictors explained between 5.4–7.5% of the variance in relationship status.

The odds ratios associated with each predictor are shown below. Positive affect was not a significant predictor, p = .365, indicating no reliable association with relationship status after controlling for the other variables.

Predictor B p OR Interpretation
Life satisfaction 0.0676 < .001 1.07 Higher life satisfaction increases odds of being in a relationship.
Positive affect –0.0146 .365 0.99 No meaningful contribution after other variables included.
Social desirability 0.1306 .014 1.14 Higher socially desirable responding increases odds of reporting being in a relationship.

Table 1: Odds Ratios for Baseline Model

Predicted probabilities were calculated to illustrate how the model translates the predictor values into the likelihood of being in a relationship. Using the mean values of all predictors, the model estimated a baseline probability of approximately 0.32, meaning that an average individual in the dataset had a 32% chance of being in a relationship. When predictor values were entered into the model individually at their mean levels, the corresponding predicted probabilities reflected the relative contribution of each variable: life satisfaction and social desirability produced higher predicted probabilities compared with the baseline estimate, whereas positive affect produced little change. Overall, the predicted probabilities were consistent with the pattern of odds ratios, indicating that only some predictors meaningfully increase the likelihood of being in a relationship.

Using a 0.50 threshold sensitivity was 94.1% and specificity was 14.7%. The model predicted “in a relationship” well but struggled to correctly identify those not in a relationship. The ROC curve yielded an AUC = 0.644. This indicates modest discrimination, above chance but not strong.

The baseline model shows that life satisfaction and social desirability are significant independent predictors of relationship status. Individuals with higher life satisfaction and higher socially desirable responding are more likely to report being in a relationship. However, prediction accuracy is limited, and the model struggles particularly with identifying individuals who are not in a relationship. Overall, the model provides statistically significant but practically modest predictive usefulness.

4.2 Model Assumptions

The Hosmer–Lemeshow test was used to evaluate the agreement between observed and predicted probabilities. The test was not statistically significant, χ²(8) = 3.53, p = .897, indicating no evidence of poor fit. This suggests that the model adequately describes the data and that predicted values closely align with observed outcomes.

Multicollinearity was assessed using Variance Inflation Factors (VIFs). All predictors had VIF values between 1.01 and 1.23 (tolerances > .80), well below conventional thresholds for concern. These results indicate that the predictors do not exhibit problematic overlap and that collinearity is unlikely to distort coefficient estimates or model interpretation.

Potential outliers and influential observations were assessed using Cook’s distance, leverage (hat) values, and DFBetas. All Cook’s distance values were below .02, and no leverage values exceeded the recommended threshold. DFBetas did not approach ±1 for any predictor, indicating that no single case exerted undue influence on the model. These findings suggest that the model estimates are stable and not disproportionately affected by individual observations.

Residuals were examined to evaluate overall model adequacy. Pearson residuals were primarily within ±2, and deviance residuals were small and symmetrically distributed, indicating no major violations of model assumptions. There was no evidence of systematic patterns or heterogeneity.

Across all diagnostic checks, baseline model met the assumptions of logistic regression. The model showed acceptable fit, no multicollinearity, no influential cases, and no residual anomalies. These results indicate that baseline modelis appropriate for interpretation, although its overall predictive performance remains modest (see Appendix 2 for plots and test output).

4.3. Summary

The baseline logistic regression model examined whether life satisfaction, positive affect, and social desirability predicted the likelihood of being in a relationship. The model was statistically significant overall and explained a modest proportion of variance (Nagelkerke R² = .075). Life satisfaction and social desirability emerged as significant positive predictors, indicating that higher scores on these psychological factors increased the odds of being in a relationship, whereas positive affect showed no meaningful contribution. Model predictions demonstrated limited practical accuracy: although sensitivity was high, specificity was extremely low, and the ROC curve indicated only modest discrimination (AUC ≈ .64).

Assumption checks showed no evidence of poor fit, multicollinearity, or influential outliers, suggesting the model was statistically appropriate. Overall, the baseline model identifies two reliable psychological predictors but provides only modest usefulness for predicting relationship status.

5. Comparison Model: Including Educational Level

This model extended the baseline model by adding education level as a categorical predictor to test whether demographic background improves prediction. No interaction terms were included here, although education was hypothesised to create differential effects on the prediction.

5.1 Model Fit

A second regression model was estimated to examine whether education level contributed additional explanatory power beyond the psychological predictors included in the baseline model. The model was statistically significant, χ²(7, N = 429) = 47.37, p < .001 with pseudo-R² values of:

  • Cox–Snell R² = .105

  • Nagelkerke R² = .145

  • Tjur’s R² = .102

Together, these values indicate that the predictors explained between 10.2%–14.5% of the variance in relationship status..

Odds ratios indicated that both pyschnological predictors meaningfully influenced the likelihood of being in a relationship:

  • Life satisfaction remained a significant positive predictor (OR = 1.08), demonstrating that each one-unit increase in life satisfaction was associated with an 8% increase in the odds of being in a relationship.

  • Social desirability also showed a small but significant positive effect (OR = 1.12), while positive affect did not contribute significantly to the model (OR ≈ 0.99).

Education level showed differential associations. Compared to respondents who completed high school (the reference category):

  • respondents with postgraduate education were more than twice as likely to be in a relationship (OR = 2.12)

  • resppndents with some additional training were 90% more likely (OR = 1.90)

  • respondents with some secondary education showed the strongest effects (OR = 7.20), indicating substantially higher odds of being in a relationship.

Predicted probabilities reflected these patterns, ranging from approximately .57 for high-school graduates to .91 for those with some secondary education.

Collectively, these results show that both psychological factors and educational attainment meaningfully shape relationship likelihood, with the latter introducing notable variability in predicted outcomes.

This model demonstrated modest predictive performance. The confusion matrix showed that the model correctly classified 41 non-relationship cases and 261 relationship cases, corresponding to an overall accuracy of approximately 70%. Sensitivity (the ability to correctly identify individuals in a relationship) was high, whereas specificity (correct identification of those not in a relationship) remained low, indicating a bias toward predicting the majority class.

The ROC curve yielded an AUC of .70, reflecting acceptable discrimination. This suggests that while the model is far from perfect, it performs meaningfully better than chance in distinguishing between individuals who are and are not in a relationship. Taken together, the classification results and AUC indicate that this model provides reasonable predictive capability, with enhanced performance relative to the baseline model, particularly when educational attainment is included as a predictor.

5.2 Assumptions Checks

Assumptions of logistic regression were evaluated to ensure that this model was appropriately specified (see Appendix 3 for plots and test output). The Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, was non-significant, χ²(8) = 2.49, p = .96, indicating that the predicted probabilities aligned well with the observed data. This result suggests that the model fits the data adequately.

Multicollinearity was examined using Generalised Variance Inflation Factors (GVIFs). All GVIF-adjusted values were close to 1 (tlifesat = 1.13; tposaff = 1.11; tmarlow = 1.01; educ = 1.01), demonstrating that there was no problematic multicollinearity among the predictors.

Outliers and influential cases were evaluated using Cook’s distance, hat values, and DFBetas. While several cases exhibited relatively higher influence statistics (Cook’s D values ≈ .04–.07 and a small number of cases showing DFBetas > |0.05|), none exceeded conventional thresholds for concern (Cook’s D > 1.0 or DFBetas > 1.0). Residual diagnostics, including Pearson and deviance residuals, showed values primarily clustered near zero with no extreme departures (Pearson residual range: approximately –2.37 to 1.34). Collectively, these results indicate that no individual observation exerted undue influence on the regression solution.

Finally, residual deviance and degrees of freedom suggested no evidence of overdispersion, and the pattern of deviance residuals did not indicate model misspecification. Overall, the diagnostic checks showed that the model met the core assumptions of logistic regression, and the model can therefore be considered appropriate and statistically reliable for interpretation.

5.3 Summary

This model shows that educational attainment improves prediction over psychological factors alone. Several education levels significantly increase the odds of being in a relationship, particularly “Some secondary” and “Postgraduate”. The model’s predictive ability is however modest.

6. Model Comparison

A comparison of the baseline model and second model was conducted to determine whether the inclusion of education level improved prediction of relationship status. The second model demonstrated a lower AIC (AIC = 514.76) compared with baseline model (AIC = 530.21), indicating a modest improvement in model fit.

The Likelihood Ratio Test also supported the enhanced fit of the comparison model: the second model showed a significantly better log-likelihood than the intercept-only model, χ²(7) = 47.37, p < .001, compared with the baseline model’s χ²(3) = 23.92, p < .001. This represents a meaningful increase in explained variance. Similarly, pseudo-R² values increased from Nagelkerke R² = .075 in the baseline to .145 in second model, indicating a substantial improvement in the model’s explanatory capability.

Changes in predictor significance revealed that the core psychological predictors, life satisfaction and social desirability, remained significant or near-significant across both models, while positive affect continued to show no predictive value. The addition of education introduced several new significant predictors, with higher educational attainment associated with increased odds of being in a relationship in some categories. This demonstrates that education captures additional relevant variance not accounted for by psychological predictors alone.

Prediction of the outcome improved slightly with education included. The second model produced a higher overall classification accuracy (approximately 70%) compared with baseline model(approximately 68%). Sensitivity increased moderately, while specificity improved from near-zero in baseline model to a modest positive value in the second model. ROC analysis showed that AUC improved from .64 in baseline model to .70 in second , indicating a shift from poor to acceptable discrimination. Diagnostic performance also improved: the second model retained non-significant Hosmer–Lemeshow tests, exhibited no concerning multicollinearity, and did not introduce undue influence from individual observations.

Overall, the second model provides a clearer, more robust, and better-performing account of relationship status than the baseline model. The improvements in AIC, pseudo-R², classification metrics, and AUC, combined with stable diagnostics, indicate that the updated model is superior to the baseline model.

7. Summary

This analysis examined the extent to which life satisfaction, positive affect, and social desirability predict the likelihood of being in a relationship, and whether education level adds explanatory value. Two logistic regression models were fitted: a baseline model including only psychological predictors and a comparison model incorporating education. The baseline model showed modest predictive ability, with life satisfaction and social desirability emerging as significant predictors. Adding education improved overall model fit, increased explained variance, and enhanced classification accuracy and discrimination. Assumption checks indicated that both models were well specified, with the second model showing particularly strong calibration and no diagnostic concerns. Overall, the comparison model provided a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of factors associated with relationship status.
